“I then reasoned in this fashion—_a posteriori_. The murderers had made their escape through one of these windows. Granted that, they could not afterward have secured the sashes from within, in the state in which they were discovered; this very obvious difficulty had brought the police examination here to a halt. Nevertheless, the sashes _were_ secured. They _must_, therefore, possess some means of fastening themselves. That inference was unavoidable. Approaching the unblocked window, I extracted the nail with some trouble and tried to lift the sash. Just as I expected, it resisted every effort. I now knew there must be a hidden spring, and this confirmation assured me that at least my starting assumptions were sound, however inexplicable the business of the nails remained. A thorough search soon disclosed the concealed spring. I pressed it and, content with this finding, refrained from lifting the sash.

“I next put back the nail and studied it closely. Anyone leaving by this window could have drawn it shut again, whereupon the spring would engage; but replacing the nail would have been impossible. The inference was clear, and restricted my inquiries still further. The murderers _must_ have departed by the second window. If, as seemed likely, the two sashes possessed identical springs, there _must_ be some difference in the nails, or at least in the manner of their fastening. I climbed onto the bedstead's sacking and examined the other window carefully over the head-board. Reaching down behind the board, I easily located and pressed its spring, which proved, as anticipated, precisely like the first. Then I inspected the nail. It was equally stout and seemed fixed in exactly the same fashion—hammered almost to its head.

“You may suppose I was perplexed; but to suppose that is to mistake the character of my reasoning. In the language of the chase, I had never once been ‘at fault.’ Not for a moment had I lost the scent. Every link of the chain remained flawless. I had followed the mystery to its final issue, and that issue was _the nail_. As I have said, it looked in every particular like its counterpart at the other window. Yet this resemblance, however decisive it appeared, counted for absolutely nothing against the fact that the clue ended here, at this very point. ‘There _must_ be some peculiarity,’ I told myself, ‘in this nail.’ I put a finger to it, and its head, together with roughly a quarter-inch of the shaft, detached itself in my hand.

Further occasions for observation were certain to present themselves. Anne soon found herself often enough with the whole four to form a judgment, though she was too prudent to confess it at home, knowing it would please neither wife nor husband. For although Louisa appeared to her somewhat preferred, she could not help believing, so far as memory and experience entitled her to judge, that Captain Wentworth loved neither sister. Their feelings for him were stronger; yet even theirs were not love. They suffered a slight fever of admiration, which might, and probably must, develop into love for someone. Charles Hayter appeared conscious of his neglect, though Henrietta sometimes seemed torn between the two men. Anne wished she could show them all what they were doing, and indicate some of the troubles into which they were venturing. She suspected no one of deceit. It gave her the greatest comfort to believe Captain Wentworth entirely unconscious of the suffering he caused. His behaviour betrayed no exultation, no miserable satisfaction in a victory. He had probably never heard of Charles Hayter's claims, nor ever considered them. His sole fault lay in receiving—for receiving was certainly the proper term—the attentions of two young ladies simultaneously.

After a brief contest, however, Charles Hayter appeared to retire. Three days went by without a single visit from him to Uppercross, a very marked alteration. He had actually declined a formal dinner invitation; and Mr. Musgrove, having found him on that occasion surrounded by large books, joined Mrs. Musgrove in declaring something must be amiss, and in speaking solemnly of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed that Henrietta had dismissed him outright, while her husband constantly relied upon his appearing the following day. Anne could only consider Charles Hayter sensible.

One morning about this period, while Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth were out shooting together, the sisters at the Cottage sat quietly over their work and received a visit at the window from the sisters at the Mansion-house.

It was an exceptionally fine November day. The Miss Musgroves crossed the little grounds and paused merely to announce that they intended taking a _long_ walk, and consequently imagined Mary would not care to accompany them. Mary, immediately piqued that they should question her walking powers, answered, “Oh yes, I should enjoy joining you exceedingly; I am very fond of walking a long way.” The expressions of both girls convinced Anne that this was the very thing they had hoped to avoid. Once again she marvelled at the obligation apparently created by the family's customs: everything must be communicated, and everything undertaken in company, however unwelcome or inconvenient that might prove.

Yet in the small town that peaceful Saturday afternoon there was no merriment. Amid sorrow and plentiful tears, the Harpers and Aunt Polly's household were being dressed in mourning. A stillness beyond the usual quiet settled over the village, though it was ordinarily quiet enough, heaven knew. The townspeople went about their business abstractedly, speaking seldom and sighing frequently. To the children the Saturday holiday felt oppressive. Their games held no pleasure, and one by one they abandoned them.

During the afternoon Becky Thatcher drifted disconsolately into the empty schoolyard, feeling deeply sad. Nothing she discovered there gave her any comfort. She said to herself:

“Oh, if I only had that brass andiron knob back! Now I haven't a single thing to remember him with.” She swallowed a small sob.

After a while she halted and murmured:

“This was the very place. Oh, if I could do it again, I'd never say that—I wouldn't say it for anything in the world. But now he's gone, and I'll never, never, never see him again.”

The thought overcame her, and she strayed away with tears running down her face. Then a considerable party of boys and girls, companions of Tom and Joe, passed by and stopped to peer over the paling fence. In hushed tones they recalled how Tom had done this or that when they last saw him, and how Joe had uttered some trifling remark, now plainly charged with terrible foreknowledge. Each child indicated precisely where the missing boys had stood, adding something of this sort: “And I was standing just like this—same as I'm standing now, with you being him—I was that close—and he smiled exactly this way—and then a kind of feeling went all through me—awful, you know—and naturally I didn't know what it meant then, but now I do!”

Next they argued over who had last seen the dead boys alive. Several claimed the melancholy honour and produced testimony more or less improved by the witnesses themselves. When at length they settled who _had_ seen the departed last and spoken the final words to them, the fortunate claimants assumed an almost holy importance, while the others stared enviously. One unfortunate boy, lacking any more impressive distinction, remembered with fairly evident pride:

“Well, Tom Sawyer gave me a licking once.”

But this attempt to win glory came to nothing. Nearly every boy could claim as much, which made the honour far too commonplace. The children slowly wandered off, still speaking with awe of their memories of the vanished heroes.
